item.title: Recording HiBar damage after other trades
item.description: When later work disturbs spray-applied protection, record the affected locations and arrange a system-specific review. A cosmetic patch should not be assumed to restore the specified assembly.

item.title: Discussing the appearance of HiBar
item.description: Appearance matters in exposed spaces, but visual choices must remain connected to the specified system. A dark or light finish does not establish material identity or fire resistance.

item.title: Commercial access planning for HiBar work
item.description: Large overhead areas may require substantial coordination even when their floor area is easy to measure. An access brief helps the contractor price the real working conditions.

item.title: HiBar delivery and material records
item.description: Product traceability begins with delivery. A simple receipt and storage routine helps the team identify what reached the site and resolve questions before installation.

item.title: Assembling a HiBar submittal pack
item.description: A submittal should connect the proposed product to the project requirements. Organise it so a reviewer can locate the relevant assembly and identify unresolved questions quickly.

item.title: The HiBar handover document checklist
item.description: A useful handover connects the installed system to its locations and acceptance records. Build the folder during the job so missing information can be resolved before the team disperses.

item.title: Photographing HiBar work responsibly
item.description: A project image can explain working conditions, but it cannot independently verify a product or rating. Use photographs as part of a traceable project record.

item.title: HiBar: the product and the assembly
item.description: Start a HiBar enquiry by identifying the building element and the purpose of the proposed work. The product name alone does not define a complete fire-resistance design.

item.title: Start a useful HiBar project enquiry
item.description: A concise enquiry helps a contractor or technical reviewer identify the next step. Include enough context to distinguish a new installation, a repair assessment and a request for product information.

item.title: Scoping a HiBar repair or replacement review
item.description: The size of a visible defect is only one part of a repair decision. Ask the project team to investigate the cause and surrounding condition before deciding how far the work should extend.

item.title: Coordinate services around HiBar-treated elements
item.description: Services and passive fire protection meet at many points in a building. A coordinated plan helps the project team distinguish different systems and avoid unreviewed changes.

item.title: Substrate questions before HiBar application
item.description: The surface receiving a spray-applied system is part of the specification. Give the project team an opportunity to review its condition and existing treatments before mobilisation.

item.title: Compare HiBar tenders on the same scope
item.description: A meaningful tender comparison checks the work behind the total. Put each proposal beside one current brief and resolve differences before selecting a contractor.

item.title: Plan HiBar thickness inspections before work starts
item.description: Inspection arrangements should be agreed before the treated surfaces become difficult to access. The design and accepted system documents establish the requirements; an article cannot prescribe a universal application thickness.

item.title: HiBar work in an occupied building
item.description: Occupation changes how a project is scheduled and handed over. Define the work zones and operational needs before the contractor proposes application arrangements.

item.title: Reading a HiBar fireproofing scope
item.description: A clear scope tells the installer and reviewer exactly which areas are included. Read it against the drawings before comparing prices or scheduling access.
